readingPaths.title: From a formal identity to an obstruction
readingPaths.description: Follow one attempted logarithm in characteristic three. The quadratic correction succeeds; a cubic class records why the next lift fails. The exposition constructs its complex and spectral sequence as they are needed.

expositions.title: Fourier, Symmetry, and Reconstruction
expositions.subtitle: Cardano, Ferrari, and categorical Fourier duality
expositions.summary: How root covers and their algebras produce Cardano's and Ferrari's substitutions, then lead to Fourier–Mukai duality, motives, and higher Galois reconstruction.
expositions.body: Starting with coefficient data, the exposition constructs root covers and uses their character decompositions, traces, and norms to derive the classical substitutions. Worked examples then connect roots to elliptic integrals, monodromy, vector bundles, point counts, and cancellation bounds, leading to motivic and spectral forms of Fourier duality.
expositions.background: The polynomial calculations use linear algebra, polynomial rings, finite group actions, and basic Galois theory. Section 2 introduces finite étale covers and torsors; the reading routes below offer a way through the calculations before returning to this geometry. Later sections use modules, sheaves, cohomology, and derived categories, with deeper theorems identified where they enter.
expositions.revision: Revised October 11, 2026: the introduction and conclusion connect the study to its companion through their shared motivic inquiry. The web edition, PDF, and TeX source agree. A companion link after the characteristic-zero qualification in section 12.4 was added on October 20, 2026 in the web, PDF and TeX editions. Prose refined October 20, 2026; the mathematical content is unchanged.
expositions.catalogueBackground: Polynomial route: linear algebra, polynomial rings, finite group actions, and basic Galois theory. Later routes use further geometric and cohomological background.
expositions.featureDetail: Concrete applications include reducing genus-two integrals to elliptic integrals, reconstructing vector bundles, counting points over finite fields, and bounding exponential sums.

expositions.title: What a Boundary Map Can Prove
expositions.subtitle: Derived gluing, torsion, Hodge inequalities, and motives
expositions.summary: Determinant lines govern tree counts, Hodge theory constrains chromatic coefficients, and an elliptic attachment reveals motivic Galois symmetries invisible in the graph.
expositions.body: A tree criterion opens a progression through derived global sections, determinant lines, and integral duality. These constructions yield arithmetic deletion–contraction and probability laws for trees and higher cells. Gysin triangles recover graph coloring cohomology; Hodge theory gives chromatic inequalities. Normalization retains attachment points, and tensor reconstruction proves that torsion and nontorsion elliptic attachments have different motivic Galois groups despite the same graph and graded cohomology. Nearby cycles lead onward to graph polynomials and periods.
expositions.background: Begin with graphs and linear algebra. Complexes, exact triangles, and derived duality are introduced through concrete constructions. The later routes use Hodge theory and motives; the geometric foundations and comparison theorems are stated where they enter the proofs.
expositions.catalogueBackground: Begin with graphs and linear algebra. Complexes, exact triangles, and derived duality enter through concrete constructions; the later routes introduce their Hodge and motivic foundations.
expositions.featureDetail: Worked examples show how torsion weighting removes a positive correlation, and how two nodal curves with the same graph can have different motivic Galois groups.
expositions.revision: Revised October 11, 2026: clarified the retained boundary data, metric probability law, Jacobian extension, and period construction; corrected two subsection headings. The web edition, PDF, and TeX source agree. Prose refined October 20, 2026; the mathematical content is unchanged.

expositions.title: What a Derivative Retains
expositions.subtitle: From side strips and oriented boundaries to infinitesimal geometry
expositions.summary: The rectangle product rule and oriented boundaries lead to Kähler differentials, cotangent complexes, higher brackets, spectral derivatives, and Goodwillie calculus, through explicit calculations.
expositions.body: Starting with side strips and a corner term, the exposition follows what successive derivatives retain. Tangent probes, ramification, Frobenius, nodal lifting obstructions and derived intersections lead to higher deformation operations, the cotangent spectra of MU and KU, and the multilinear layers of Goodwillie calculus.
expositions.background: Begin with the product rule, rectangles, and oriented boundaries. Polynomial rings and modules enter with Kähler differentials; complexes and homology enter with constraints and derived intersections. Later sections state the characteristic, grading, and comparison hypotheses needed for deformation theory, spectra, and Goodwillie calculus.
expositions.catalogueBackground: Begin with calculus, polynomial rings, and oriented boundaries. Later sections introduce complexes and homology, then use formal deformation theory, spectra, and homotopy functors.
expositions.featureDetail: Worked examples distinguish an invisible Frobenius direction, a node’s lifting obstruction, derived self-intersection, and the K-theory and rational data retained by spectral derivatives.
expositions.revision: First published October 17, 2026. Revised October 17, 2026 with clarifications in sections 5, 6, 12 and 13. The matching PDF edition of 39 pages and downloadable Markdown reflect the revised reading edition. A short companion link was added to section 7 on October 20, 2026, in the web, Markdown and PDF editions. Prose refined October 20, 2026; the mathematical content is unchanged.

expositions.title: When a Formal Logarithm Fails
expositions.subtitle: Corrections, cohomology, and a spectral sequence in characteristic three
expositions.summary: An attempted formal logarithm produces a quadratic correction and a cubic obstruction. A filtered cobar complex identifies the failure as a nonzero spectral sequence differential.
expositions.body: The multiplicative law supplies a coproduct. Its normalized cobar complex organizes successive corrections, and a total-weight filtration exposes a nonzero second differential. A Witt-vector addition law gives the obstruction polynomial a further use.
expositions.background: Begin with formal power series and linear algebra over a field. Cochain complexes, filtrations and the required spectral sequence are constructed in the text; the final interpretation uses exact triangles.
expositions.catalogueBackground: Formal power series and linear algebra. The text develops the cochain complex, filtration and spectral sequence used in the calculation.
expositions.revision: First published October 20, 2026. The web, PDF, Markdown and TeX editions contain the same argument.

expositions.title: Quotients, Refinement, and Reconstruction
expositions.subtitle: From exact Mal’cev categories to homotopy and linearization
expositions.summary: One comparison of quotients yields refinement, Jordan–Hölder, and invariance of dimension. Extensions, probes, and higher quotients then reveal what the simple factors leave undetermined.
expositions.body: A common quotient construction compares filtrations in pointed exact Mal’cev categories, with groups and modules as instances. Comparison pages, extensions, nilpotent probes, and Hall multiplication lead onward to coherent quotients, descent, and linearization.
expositions.background: Begin with groups, vector spaces, and their maps. The ordinary categorical comparison is developed from stated axioms. The later routes introduce module calculations and complexes, then use spaces, derived categories, and explicitly cited higher foundations.
expositions.catalogueBackground: Groups, vector spaces, and their maps. Read §§1–4.5 for the common comparison and dimension theorem; later routes state their further prerequisites.
expositions.revision: First published October 2026. The October 22 clarification edition makes three explanatory steps explicit. Further discussion appears in the notes on proofs, dependencies, and revisions. The complete web text and 82-page PDF have matching section and theorem numbers; the TeX archive contains the corresponding manuscript inputs.
expositions.featureDetail: Worked calculations compare finite bases and simple layers, distinguish extensions with the same factors, recover nilpotent chain lengths, and count flags to obtain Hall multiplication.

expositions.title: Six Elements, One Comparison
expositions.subtitle: A teaching companion to Quotients, Refinement and Reconstruction
expositions.summary: Follow addition modulo six through quotient maps, the comparison rectangle, refinement and factor matching, with seven exercises, worked answers and a guide to the higher chapters.
expositions.body: A concrete first route through the quotient comparison. The same six elements accompany each construction, followed by an optional spectral calculation and a staged guide to the main exposition.
expositions.background: Subgroups and cosets suffice for the main route. The categorical language is introduced after its role is visible. Read §§1–8 first; §9 and the higher-chapter routes are optional.
expositions.catalogueBackground: Subgroups and cosets. A concrete C₆ route through the main exposition, with exercises and worked answers.

expositions.title: A Weighting Argument for Pointwise Convergence to Convergence in Measure
expositions.summary: How a positive measurable weight turns almost-everywhere convergence into convergence in measure, with an Egorov construction and a shorter dominated-convergence proof.
expositions.body: The note follows a simple idea: control a sequence by changing its scale at each point. It develops both a countable-decomposition argument and a proof through dominated convergence.
expositions.background: Measure theory and convergence of measurable functions.
expositions.revision: Revised September 22, 2026: clarified positive indexing, the convention for empty suprema, and the domain of the measurable envelope.

expositions.title: IBM Ponder This July 2010
expositions.summary: A rounding problem becomes a congruence problem through algebraic traces, recurrences, and a companion matrix.
expositions.body: This solution to the July 2010 IBM Ponder This challenge moves between algebraic numbers and finite arithmetic. Traces provide an integer recurrence, and a companion matrix organizes the modular calculation.
expositions.background: Algebraic numbers, polynomial roots, and modular arithmetic.

references.label: IBM: the original challenge and solution
references.description: IBM's July 2010 page includes Henry Shin in its list of solvers.

expositions.title: Divisibility of Separated Polynomials
expositions.summary: A criterion explaining when divisibility of two-variable polynomial differences forces composition with a common one-variable polynomial.
expositions.body: The argument uses a residue expansion in a free module, followed by a reduction along the diagonal. A companion exposition revisits the same criterion through Galois theory and Frobenius descent.
expositions.background: Polynomial rings and basic field theory.
expositions.revision: Revised September 22, 2026: added a full fiber-constancy criterion over arbitrary fields, using Hasse derivatives to retain inseparable multiplicities. The original composition theorem and its free-module proof are unchanged.

expositions.title: A Galois-Theoretic and Frobenius-Descent Viewpoint on a Polynomial Composition Law
expositions.summary: A second approach to the separated-polynomial composition criterion, using Galois theory and reduction in positive characteristic.
expositions.body: Generic fibers and descent give another way to understand the composition law. The positive-characteristic part isolates the role of Frobenius. Read this alongside Divisibility of Separated Polynomials.
expositions.background: Galois theory and polynomials in positive characteristic.
expositions.revision: Revised September 22, 2026: clarified the nontriviality conditions in the closing reducibility discussion and the remainder argument when the outer polynomial is zero. The composition theorem and its hypotheses are unchanged.

expositions.title: Normality, Coherent Extension, Tensor Operations, and Affineness
expositions.summary: Solutions to Hartshorne II.5.14–18 connecting projective normality, coherent sheaves, affine morphisms, and vector bundles.
expositions.body: These notes bring together exercises 14 through 18 in Chapter II, Section 5 of Hartshorne’s Algebraic Geometry. The emphasis is on the relationships between the constructions: normalization and section rings, coherent extension, tensor operations, relative Spec, and vector bundles.
expositions.background: Schemes, coherent sheaves, and the material of Hartshorne II.5.
expositions.revision: Revised September 22, 2026: clarified the nonempty-scheme and rank-zero conventions, independence of lifts in the associated graded, and the local arguments underlying section-ring finiteness, coherent extension, relative Spec, and bundle sections.

expositions.title: Extracting the First Prime Greater than m
expositions.summary: An explicit finite formula selects the smallest prime above a given integer using factorial congruences, greatest common divisors, and valuations.
expositions.body: The construction turns tests for primality into a formula that isolates the first prime beyond a prescribed integer. The point is the exact arithmetic mechanism, rather than a practical prime-search algorithm.
expositions.background: Elementary number theory, factorials, and divisibility.
expositions.revision: Revised October 7, 2026: clarified the introduction while preserving the problem’s IRC provenance. The theorem, proof, and appendix are unchanged.

expositions.title: A Note on Disjoint Decompositions of [0,1) into Closed Sets
expositions.summary: A proof that a half-open interval cannot be partitioned into countably many sets closed in the real line.
expositions.body: The distinction between being closed in the real line and relatively closed in an interval matters here. The note develops the obstruction using point-set topology and Baire category.
expositions.background: Closed sets and the Baire category theorem.
expositions.revision: Revised September 22, 2026: explicitly established that the closed remainder is nonempty before applying the Baire category theorem.

expositions.title: Lebesgue's Criterion for Riemann Integrability
expositions.summary: A compactness proof that a bounded function is Riemann integrable when its discontinuities form a set of measure zero.
expositions.body: The argument connects a local condition on discontinuities with the upper and lower sums of Riemann integration. Compactness supplies the finite control needed to finish the proof.
expositions.background: Riemann integration, compactness, and sets of measure zero.
expositions.revision: Revised September 22, 2026: included the zero-length interval, corrected two strict oscillation bounds to non-strict bounds, and supplied a direct Darboux proof of the composition corollary that uses neither direction of Lebesgue’s criterion. Revised October 7, 2026: clarified overlapping covers and closed-cell estimates, and developed the Thomae and Cantor-set examples.

expositions.title: Products Preserve Riemann Integrability
expositions.summary: A local oscillation estimate turns the product-difference identity into a Darboux proof that products of Riemann integrable functions are integrable.
expositions.body: The note compares two values of a product on a small interval, bounds their difference using the oscillations of the factors, and sums over a common refinement. Diagrams illustrate the estimate and the passage from local variation to a global integrability criterion.
expositions.background: Bounded functions, upper and lower Darboux sums, and partition refinement.
expositions.revision: Revised September 22, 2026: the product proof chooses positive bounds for the factors, making its strict estimate valid also when both functions vanish. Nonempty intervals are explicit. Revised October 7, 2026: condensed the explanatory prose and made the hypotheses of the concluding Lipschitz principle explicit.

expositions.title: Selected Problems in Discrete Mathematics and Analysis
expositions.summary: Six problems on counting, arithmetic progressions, recurrences, infinite series, and the information supplied by different observation rules.
expositions.body: A collection of six problem statements, presented without solutions. They range from finite counting arguments to the asymptotic behavior of an infinite series.
expositions.background: Counting, elementary number theory, recurrences, and convergence of series.
expositions.revision: Revised September 22, 2026: Problem 2 specifies a disjoint partition with distinct moduli greater than one; Problem 5 has the corrected series value; and Problem 6 distinguishes three recorded outcomes from an exact-onset timing variant.

puzzles.title: Cube patterns
puzzles.summary: Hearts and pixel figures on a cube, made for fun with my own move sequences.
puzzles.galleryIntro: Hearts and little pixel figures, made with move sequences I worked out on large twisty cubes.
puzzles.body: I work out my own move sequences on large twisty cubes, using commutators to rearrange small groups of pieces, then combining the sequences to make hearts and little pixel figures. The puzzle is to build up the picture without undoing the parts already in place. Finding the moves is part of the enjoyment.

broodWar.title: StarCraft: Brood War
broodWar.body:
I play StarCraft: Brood War, lately especially on Fastest Possible maps. I enjoy the scale and pace of these games: keeping production moving, reading the map, bringing together units with different roles, and finding the moment to act with teammates. The generous resources make it possible to set a great deal in motion. Much of the pleasure lies in deciding where attention matters next, and how one action can prepare the way for another.

I’ve begun collecting some of these games on YouTube, with in-game audio and no commentary.

overwatch.title: Overwatch
overwatch.body:
I’ve also played Overwatch as RiemannRoch. In the original game I reached Master, mainly playing Zarya and other tanks; in Overwatch 2 I reached Diamond 5 while learning Support. I queued on my own for both.

With a different mix of teammates each match, part of the challenge was reading the team as we played: when to push together, what help to expect, and how to coordinate without having practiced together.
